FOREWORD This Indian Standard was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Food Analysis and Nutrition Sectional Committee had been approved by the Food and Agriculture Division Council. Ice-cream the main procedure properties cream'. is a widely consumed food. A consumer judges its quality on the basis of its sensory characteristics, ones being appearance, colour, body and texture and flavour. This standard specifies an acceptable for sensory evaluation to the manufacturers and consumers for evaluating the product for its sensory on a rational basis. The specifications of ice cream are covered in IS 2802:1964 `Specification for ice

For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the final value, observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test or analysis, shall be rounded off in accordance with IS 2:1960 `Rules for rounding off numerical values (revised)'. The number of significant places retained in the rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard.

1 SCOPE This standard prescribes conditions, technique, method and evaluating card for sensory evaluation of ice cream. 2 REFERENCES The following standards contain provisions, which through reference in this text, constitute provisions of this standard. 3.1.6 Ofl-Sweetening -- Lacks sweetness, too sweet, unnatural sweetness. An ice cream lacking in sweetness or too sweet is noted readily upon tasting, the former tending to give a flat taste whereas the latter may exhibit candy sweetness. Unnatural sweetness is characteristic of sweeteners. 3.1.7 Salty -- Although encountered is associated with a high percentage not-fat. occasionally, it of milk solids-

3.1.8 Gummy -- Association with a doughy condition as evidenced by a marked tendency of the ice cream to curl up behind the dipper leaving coarse, deep, irregular waves. 3.1.9 Soggy, Heavy -- Associated with high solids or use of excessive amounts of stabilizer and low overrun. Evidenced by a much colder sensation of ice cream on the mouth than free of this defect. 3.1.10 Shrunken -- A shrunken ice cream manifests itself by being withdrawn from the sides of the container. It is associated with low solids much stabilizer and low overrun. 3.1.11 Weak, Watery -- A characteristic which is associated with a low melting resistance, a thin, milky, low; viscosity melt. 3.1.12 l?utte~, Greasy -- Associated with the presence of butter particles in the mouth after the ice cream has been melted on by a greasy coating of the linings of the mouth after expectoration. 3.1.13 Coarse, Grainy, Ice-- Characterized by general lack of smooth, velvety character, and feeling of unusual coldness in the mouth. 3.1.14 Flaky, Snowy -- Such ice cream manifests itself by a tendency to fall apart when dipped. This condition is associated with low solids, low stabilizer and high over-run. 3.1.15 Ffufi, Foamy, S"ongy -- Closely associated with high over-run and high melting resistance. 3.1.16 Sandy -- A characteristic of ice cream having fine, hard, uniform, sand like particles of lactose. The presence of these sand like particles is noted by pressing a thin layer of ice cream against the roof of 1

.3 TERMINOLOGY 3.1 For the purpose of this standard, the following definitions in addition to those giveninIS5126 (Part 1) and IS 5126 (Part 2) shall apply. 3.1.1 Old Ingredient, Old, Stale, Musty -- This is associated with the use of old ingredients, which have undergone chemical changes and is suggestive of uncleanliness. 3.1.2 Egg -- A characteristic which is typical of egg yolk and somewhat resembles the cooked of custard flavour. 3.1.3 High Acid, Sour -- Associated with the development of lactic acid in one or more of the dairy products used or by holding the mix at a favorable growth temperature for bacteria for a long time. 3.1.4 Metallic, Oily -- Associated with the development of oxidation of unsaturated glycerides of fat. Refers to flavour resembling machine oil. 3.1.5 Unnatural -- A characteristic associated with the flavour extracts prepared by improper balancing of constituents used in the preparation of the extract. For example synthetic vanillin, often used to fortify

IS 15349:2003 the mouth with the tongue to secure quick melting. 3.1.17 Flaky or Scummy -- Manifested by a feathery, light-colored scum on the surface after melting. 3.1.18 Foamy or Frothy -- Associated with ice cream, which on completed melting shows many large bubbles 1/8 to 3/16 of an inch diameter. 3.1.19 cream watery solids Watery, Low Melting Resistance -- Such ice melts quickly, the resulting melt being of a thin, consistency. Commonly associated with low in the mix and a coarse, weak body. 5.2.1.4 Oxidized jlavour Prepare ice cream from mix to which 1 to 2 mg/kg chloride of iron or copper has been added. 5.2.1.5 Coarse, icy, weak Prepare ice cream without using a stabilizer. 5.2.1.6 Crumbly Prepare ice cream having a low total solids content, low amount of stabilizer, low homogenization pressure (around 1000 and 500 pounds per square inch) and excessive over-run (100 percent over-run). 5.2.1.7 Fh@ Prepare ice cream having low total solids, low stabilizer and high over-run. 5.2.1.8 Sandy Prepare ice cream having excessively high SNF content. Draw ice cream fiorn the freezer at a relatively high temperature (say 12"C). Harden it in hardening cabinets having high temperature (�1O"C approximately) and shut off the power supply intermittently so as to have fluctuating temperatures. 5.2.1.9 Soggy Prepare ice cream having high total solids, excessive amount of stabilizer (0.5 percent), and low over-run. 5.2.1.10 Gummy Prepare ice cream having excessive amount of stabilizer (0.5 percent) and sweetener (15 percent). 5.2.1.11 Curdv . melt down 5.2 Training 5.2.1 Preparation of Ice Cream Samples for Training Prepare ice cream from mix having high acidity and which has been homogenized at excessively high pressures (3 500 and 500 pounds per square inch). A small quantity of calcium chloride solution may also be added to induce this defect. 5.2.2 Procedure for Training 5.2.2.1 The panelists should be familiarized with all the desirable characteristics of ice cream. They should be trained ,to.distinguish between coarse and sandy samples. They should also be trained to distinguish samples with common defec~, such as old ingredient oxidized/metallic flavours, coarse, ice, week crumbly, flu~, sandy, soggy, gummy body and texture and ctirdy melt down. 5.2.2.2 A series of 20 judgments should be obtained from each prospective panelist utilizing a pair of samples with known differences. To compensate for the known variations fi-om day-to-day a qualifying test is given for a 3.day period. Those who make an acceptile (75 percent ccirreet score should be chosen).
L

3.1.20 Unnatural Colour -- A characteristic of ice cream having grey, dull, pale, vivid, chalky, not uniform colour. 4 GENERAL CONDITIONS

The conditions of sensory evaluation of ice cream shall be as given in IS 6273 (Part 1). 5 PANELISTS 5.1 Selection Persons with normal sensitivity for taste and odour should be selected. They should have ability to detect small differences between paired samples with minor flavour, colour or textural differences. They should be able to recognize the primary stimuli like sweet, sour, salty and bitter. Selection among the available panelists should be based on their significant capacity to distinguish quality variations and other attributes. Those who dislike ice cream or any other milk products should be excluded from the panel.

A control sample of fresh ice cream (prepared under standard condition from fresh milk ingredients) representing desirable characteristics like flavour, body and texture, melting resistance and colour should be served alongwith the sample having one or more of the following defects in different intensities. 5.2.1.1 Lacks flavouring Prepare ice cream without the addition of flavoring at the time of freezing. 5.2.1.2 Lacks sweetness Prepare ice cream having less than 12 percent sugar. 5.2.1.3 Old ingredient Prepare ice cream using off-flavoured ingredients like skim milk powder which has been stored for more than a year, and cream which has developed yeasty, cheesy, musty and bitter flavour. .

IS 15349:2003 5.2.2.3 The panelists should be checked once in three months for their consistency and acuity. 5.3 Number of Panelists the mouth, roll it between the incisors and bring them together very gently, noting the ice crystal. Note also whether grittiness is apparent between the teeth. A small portion between the incisors may reveal the presence of minute traces of a gritty or sandy texture. When the sample is liquefied and warmed to body temperature, the detection of the flavour is not difficult. It is best accomplished by placing a small teaspoonful or bite of the ice cream directly into the mouth, quickly manipulating the sample between the teeth and palate and noting the taste and odour sensations. Note if the sample leaves any after-taste. By the time the flavour has been determined, the samples, previously set aside for melting, which have softened sufficiently to yield an accurate picture of the melting characteristics. The judge should observe whether the ice cream has retained its form and approximate size; whether the melted liquid is creamy, curdled, foamy or watery. 7.2 Method Follow composite scoring method as described in 4.2.8 of IS 6273 (Part 2). 7.3 Evaluation in one session should not Card `

Five to seven panelists should be employed in the evaluation to arrive at consistent and statistically valid results. At least 10 judgments should be taken. 6 SAMPLING, PRESENTATION 6.1 Sampling A representative sample should be drawn from the lot. Precautions should be taken to avoid an extraneous contamination in drawing, handling and presentation of samples. 6.2 Preparation of Sample removing ice cream from the temper it at �12� to �15�C for PREPARATION AND

Immediately after hardening cabinet, judging. 6.3 Amount

of Each Samples

A sample of about 100 ml should be sufficient. 6.4 Number The number exceed five. 6.5 Coding Coding of samples should be done as recommended under 7 of IS 6273 (Part 1). 7 PROCEDURE 7.1 Technique of Testing of Samples of samples

Use the evaluation card given in Table 1 for recording observations for reconstituted malted milk. Calculate the final score by deducting score under Section B from score under Section A. 7.4 Grading After computation of data recorded in Table 1 by the panelists the following grades should be given to the sample evaluated: Total Score 90 and above 80-89 70-79 69 and above 7.5 Statistical Evaluation Grade Excellent Good Fair Poor of Results

Note the colour, condition of the container. During the actual dipping of the sample, note carefully the way the product cuts and the feel of the dipper as its cutting edge passes through the frozen mass. Note particularly whether the ice cream tends to curl up or roll in semated layers behind the dipper or spoon thus indicating excessive gumminess or stickiness.
